source: Cammeraat, Rop and de Koning (2020) The influence of spatial distance and signaling on the split-attention effect, Computers in Human Behavior 105, 106203
finding: Full text opened. This URL is the Cammeraat paper itself, not Pouw 2019 (so line a18 carries the wrong URL). Exp 1 crossed distance (small, large) with colour signaling. Distance had no effect on recall, transfer or mental effort. Signaling helped only the items that were colour-coded.
numbers: Exp 1: N=107 psychology students, 4 groups of 26-27. Free recall: distance F<1, signaling F<1, interaction F(1,103)=1.60; BF for null 4.72 (distance), 4.80 (signaling), 22.94 (interaction). Transfer: all F<1, BF null 4.40, 4.74, 19.91. Mental effort after learning: BF null 3.46 (distance), 3.64 (signaling). Signaled label items: signaling F(1,103)=3.29, partial eta2=.06, BF alt only 2.66 (anecdotal).
quote: Distance had no effect on recall, transfer or mental effort
limits: Students in a lab, one car-brake text. Signaling effect is on the colour-coded items only. The paper itself says small distance may already be enough, so large distance is the open question.
agent_relevance: Spatial distance alone did not matter here, but a cue that tells the reader what goes with what helped the cued items. For a prompt: a tag that links item to rule is worth more than moving text.

source: Cammeraat, Rop and de Koning (2020), Experiment 2 (the replication of Johnson and Mayer 2012)
finding: Experiment 2 reused the Johnson and Mayer 2012 integrated and separated materials. It found no split-attention effect on any outcome. The authors say this raises doubts about how robust the effect is and that the CLT account (more load when separated) is not supported by the effort ratings.
numbers: Exp 2: 180 Mechanical Turk workers recruited, 140 in analysis (df 2,137), 3 groups (integrated n=48, separated signaling n=49, separated n=43). Free recall F(2,137)=1.91, p=.153, BF null 5.11. Signaled label items F=1.22, BF null 3.45. Non-signaled label items F=2.18, BF alt 1.70 (anecdotal). Transfer F<1, BF null 12.04 (strong). Mental effort learning: integrated 7.33, separated signaling 7.45, separated 7.67 (scale 1-9). A reviewer-requested t-test of integrated vs separated was also n.s.
limits: Online sample, unsupervised, so noise is higher than in the lab. The authors judged this explanation unlikely. Null result for one material set only.
agent_relevance: The textbook contrast (integrated vs separated) can fail to replicate even with the same materials. Do not assume an integration gain for the agent; measure it on our own tasks.

source: Kalyuga, Chandler and Sweller (1999) Managing split-attention and redundancy in multimedia instruction, Applied Cognitive Psychology 13 (re-read to reconcile F values)
finding: Re-read to settle the number mismatch flagged in the critique. The F values are consistent. In Exp 2 (colour coding), F(1,13)=2.42 is the training-time difference (n.s.), which is why instruction time was used as a covariate. After that: multiple-choice F(1,13)=7.17, subjective load F(1,13)=3.09 (marginal), fault-finding F(1,13)=0.78 (n.s.), effectiveness F(1,13)=7.01. In Exp 1 (audio/visual text and redundancy), F(2,31)=4.86 fault finding, F(2,31)=7.80 questions.
numbers: Exp 1: 34 learners (df 2,31), groups of 11 to 12. Exp 2: 16 learners (df 1,13). Exp 1 post-hoc: audio-text group beat visual-plus-audio on all measures; audio beat visual text on fault finding and questions.
quote: The colour-coding technique can be used to eliminate the problems associated with split-attention
limits: Very small N, trade apprentices, computer-based, same lab as the founders. Colour coding helped the multiple-choice items but not fault finding. The authors say fault finding may need only remembered locations.
agent_relevance: Closes the Kalyuga re-check. Colour cues helped understanding items but not a task that could be done from memory of locations, so a cross-reference cue may help only tasks that need real linking.

source: Chandler and Sweller (1992) The split-attention effect as a factor in the design of instruction, British Journal of Educational Psychology 62 (abstract level only)
finding: Full text could not be opened: the publisher page returned 403 and the core.ac.uk links returned HTML, not a PDF. At abstract level (from a search result): two experiments, the first with Numerical Control programming, found integrated formats better than conventional split-source formats for technical and textual material. The electrical-engineering results with six experiments are in the 1991 paper (Cognition and Instruction), where one wiring experiment found no difference when mental integration was not needed.
numbers: No experiment-level numbers obtained. Do not quote figures from this paper.
limits: Abstract-level only, from a search snippet. Gap 8 stays open for this paper.
agent_relevance: Origin of the integrate-where-used rule, but our design should rest on later meta-analyses and the replication record (d01, d02), not on this paper.

source: Anthropic (2026) Prompting best practices for current Claude models: long context prompting
finding: The vendor guidance for our model family says: put long documents at the top of the prompt, above the query, instructions and examples; put the query at the end; ask the model to quote relevant parts first for long-document tasks. The page gives the 30 percent figure but with no study, model or task behind it.
numbers: Claim on page: queries at the end can improve response quality by up to 30 percent in tests, especially with complex, multidocument inputs. Applies to inputs of about 20K tokens or more. Page lists current models up to Fable 5.1 and Sonnet 5.5.
quote: Queries at the end can improve response quality by up to 30 percent in tests
limits: Vendor claim without published method. Treat as a prior, not as evidence. It is about long documents; it does not test inline-versus-header rule placement.
agent_relevance: Direct, model-specific advice: data first, task last, quote-then-answer. Matches Ok and Lee (d07) and Leviathan (d06). Test it once on our own tasks.

source: Leviathan, Kalman and Matias (2025) Prompt Repetition Improves Non-Reasoning LLMs, arXiv 2512.14982
finding: Repeating the whole prompt (query, query) raised accuracy of seven models when reasoning was off, with no loss anywhere. The authors' explanation is causal attention: later tokens can see earlier ones but not the reverse, so a second copy lets every token see every other. A padding control (periods up to the same length) did not help, so the gain is not length. With step-by-step reasoning on, the effect was neutral to slightly positive.
numbers: 7 models (Gemini 2.0 Flash and Flash Lite, GPT-4o and 4o-mini, Claude 3 Haiku and 3.7 Sonnet, DeepSeek V3), 7 benchmarks: wins 47 of 70 model-benchmark tests (McNemar p<0.1), 0 losses. Gemini 2.0 Flash-Lite on NameIndex 21.33% to 97.33%. With reasoning: 5 wins, 1 loss, 22 ties of 28. Options-first multiple choice gained most, question-first gained little. Anthropic models had higher latency on very long repeated prompts.
quote: repeating the input prompt improves performance for popular models
limits: Models are early-2025 and not our current ones. p<0.1 threshold. Two custom benchmarks drive the largest gains. Not tested at long document scale with frontier reasoning on.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: when the model is not reasoning, putting the task after the material or repeating it is a reliable gain, and the gain is from visibility, not length. With reasoning on, little to gain.

source: Ok and Lee (2026) Lost in the Prompt Order: Revealing the Limitations of Causal Attention in Language Models, Findings of ACL 2026
finding: Full text opened. Putting the context before the question and options (CQO) beats the reverse (QOC) in multiple-choice QA by a large margin. Mechanism: under the causal mask, option tokens in QOC cannot see the context. Fixes that work without touching the model: repeat the options after the context (QOCO) and chain-of-thought. The gap also holds for a current commercial model.
numbers: 21 decoder-only open models (Llama 3, Qwen 2.5/3, Gemma 2; base and instruct), 4 datasets. Average CQO 69.26 vs QOC 54.54 (about 14.7 points). QOCO repeat: QOC +8.2 points (to 62.76). Activation patching +6.0. CoT: gap shrinks to 7.47 points on average. Appendix E, Gemini-3-Flash-preview, no thinking: CQO 87.4, QOC 75.5, gap 11.84 points; CoT closes 83.4% of the gap (open models: 49.2%).
quote: placing context before the questions and options (CQO) outperforms the reverse order (QOC) by over 14%p
limits: Multiple-choice QA with short options; the open models are small to mid size. One closed model, one provider. The gap is about question and options placement, not about rule placement.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 and gap 2 (partly): a current frontier-class model still shows an order penalty of about 12 points when the task comes first. Put material first, then task and options; repeat the options or reason first.

source: Modarressi et al. (2025) NoLiMa: Long-Context Evaluation Beyond Literal Matching, ICML 2025 (arXiv 2502.05167)
finding: With no word overlap between question and needle, accuracy falls fast with length even for strong models. Newer models (GPT-4.1) help but the pattern holds. Giving answer options (a literal cue) restores most of the loss; two-hop items fall much faster than one-hop items.
numbers: Base score then 32K (and 128K). GPT-4o: base 99.3, 8K 89.2, 32K 69.7, 128K 56.0. GPT-4.1: base 97.0, 32K 79.8, 64K 69.7, 128K 64.7. Gemini 2.0 Flash: 89.4 base, 32K 41.0, 128K 16.4. Claude 3.5 Sonnet: 87.5 base, 32K 29.8. 11 of 13 models fell below 50% of base at 32K. Llama 3.3 70B ablation at 8K/16K/32K: direct question 98.3/98.5/98.5; one-hop 84.1/73.2/56.2; one-hop with multiple-choice cue 98.7/97.4/93.1; two-hop 57.4/42.7/25.9; two-hop with cue 96.3/94.6/87.2. Reasoning models (o1, o3-mini, R1) on the 10 hardest pairs fell below 50% at 32K.
limits: Synthetic needle tests, latent association required. Models are 2024 to early 2025. No Claude 4+ or Gemini 2.5 Pro / GPT-5 class models in the main table.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 6: current-generation models still lose a lot when the link between question and fact is implicit, and an explicit cue ties them back. Gap 7: harm scales with the number of hops, as element interactivity predicts. An explicit tag linking item to rule is the analogue of that cue.

source: Chroma research (2025) Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance (technical report)
finding: Report on 18 current models (Claude Opus 4, Sonnet 4, 3.7, 3.5, Haiku 3.5; o3, GPT-4.1 family, GPT-4o; Gemini 2.5 Pro, 2.5 Flash, 2.0 Flash; Qwen3). Performance falls as input grows in every experiment, and the drop is not due to the needle-question pair being hard. Lower needle-question similarity degrades faster. Even one distractor lowers accuracy; four compound it. A shuffled haystack beat a coherent one in all 18 models. On conversational memory, a focused ~300-token input beat the full ~113k-token input for every model.
numbers: LongMemEval: 306 prompts, full ~113k tokens vs focused ~300 tokens; all models scored higher on focused. Needle-question similarity 0.445 to 0.775 (essays), 0.521 to 0.829 (arXiv). Needle position showed no notable effect in this setup. Exact accuracies are in charts, not text.
limits: Read through a fetch-and-summarize tool, so figures are what the summary returned; the report's chart values were not extracted. Company technical report, not peer reviewed. Mostly older Claude models.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 3: current-generation models still degrade with length and with distractors, and clean short input wins. Coherent text hurt more than shuffled text, which points to content, not only length.

source: Bianchi et al. (2025) Hidden in the Haystack: Smaller Needles Are More Difficult for LLMs to Find, arXiv 2505.18148 v2
finding: Eleven models, over 150K controlled runs, three benchmarks. The shorter the gold passage, the worse the accuracy, and the more sensitive to position. This holds after controlling for position, answer repetition, gold-to-distractor ratio, distractor volume and domain. So size of the needed fact is its own factor, apart from position and total length.
numbers: CARDBiomedBench: Gemini 2.0 Flash 48% (small gold), 62% (medium), 73% (large); GPT-4o 77% to 98%; Llama 3.1 405B 74% to 92%. Gold-only baselines 96% (Gemini 2.0 Flash), 100% (GPT-4o, Llama 405B). Position: small gold at start 94%, near end 33% for Gemini 2.0 Flash (61-point drop); large gold 84% to 65%. NuminaMath tested with 5, 10, 15 distractors (about 25K, 50K, 75K tokens): gold size still dominant.
limits: Models are 2024 to early 2025 (including Gemini 2.5 Flash and reasoning models in the set). Synthetic insertion of gold passages into distractor documents.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a partial three-way split exists. Size of the needed fact, its position and the distractor volume each matter on their own. A short rule buried in long text is the worst case, which argues for keeping short rules next to the case or at the edges.

source: Gao, Chen and Huang (2026) The First Drop of Ink: Nonlinear Impact of Distracting Information in Long-Context Reasoning, ICML 2026 (arXiv 2605.10828 v2)
finding: At fixed context length, the first 10% of hard distractors causes most of the damage; the rest adds little. Hard distractors are topical passages without the answer. A theory based on softmax attention says the gold passage's share of attention is a convex function of hard-distractor share. A controlled filtering test shows that most recovery from filtering is from shorter context, not from removing the hard items, until hard share is near zero.
numbers: Models: Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-Next-80B, up to 128K tokens; NQ, TriviaQA, PopQA, HotpotQA; 200 examples each. Drop ratio (share of total loss in the first 10% hard) is 0.58 for Qwen2.5-7B on nq easy at 128K; linear would be 0.1. With 100 distractor docs, adding 10% hard cut attention on the gold by 76%. Filter Hard vs Filter Random gave nearly identical gains from removing the first 80K tokens; they diverge below about 47K tokens, where hard share goes to near zero.
quote: filtering gains mainly come from context-length reduction rather than distractor removal
limits: Open models up to 80B, not frontier closed models. Substring match was replaced by an LLM judge (gpt-4o-mini). Retrieval-style QA with a single gold passage.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 and 4: a few near-miss items do most of the harm, and half-hearted filtering mainly helps by shortening. A code-side filter must remove the near-misses nearly completely or it is only a length cut.

source: Dhara and Sheth (2026) Context-Length Robustness in Question Answering Models: A Comparative Empirical Study, MathAI 2026 (arXiv 2603.15723)
finding: A controlled test that keeps the answer-bearing signal (256 tokens) fixed and pads with irrelevant text. Multi-hop QA (HotpotQA) loses far more than single-span QA (SQuAD). The larger model is better but degrades in the same pattern.
limits: Small n (about 1.7-point steps), two models of one family, contexts only to 2048 tokens, exact match. Low-profile paper by industry authors.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: supports that clean-up gains concentrate in multi-part items (element interactivity). Even a 2048-token context costs a gpt-4.1 model 27 points on multi-hop items. A G12 stratified test is worth running.

source: Rajeev et al. (2025) Cats Confuse Reasoning LLM: Query-Agnostic Adversarial Triggers for Reasoning Models, COLM 2025 (arXiv 2503.01781)
finding: Appending one irrelevant, query-agnostic sentence (for example a fact about cats) to math problems raises error rates of reasoning models. Triggers found on DeepSeek V3 transferred to R1 and to other families. Harm is by content, since the sentence is very short, so it is not a length effect.
numbers: Search: 1618 problems usable, 574 broke the proxy (35%); 114 transferred to R1 (about 20%). Three fixed triggers combined: R1 error rate 4.50% vs random baseline 1.50% (3 times); R1-distill-Qwen-32B 8.00% (2.83 times). Abstract: error rate up by up to 500% for reasoning models and 700% for instruction-tuned models across Qwen QwQ, Qwen3, Phi-4, Llama-3.1, Mistral. Slowdown (response at least 1.5 times longer): o1 26.4%, o3-mini 16.8%, R1 28.0%, R1-distill 42.2% of adversarial prompts.
quote: appending Interesting fact: cats sleep most of their lives to any math problem leads to more than doubling the chances of a model getting the answer wrong
limits: Adversarially searched triggers, not natural clutter. Absolute rates are low (a few percent). Only 60% of modified problems judged consistent with the original.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 3: current reasoning models can be thrown by one irrelevant sentence, and it also makes them think longer (cost). Argues for stripping non-task sentences in code before the model sees them.

source: Mirzadeh et al. (2025) GSM-Symbolic, ICLR 2025: GSM-NoOp drops for newer models (figure values)
finding: Re-opened to get the per-model GSM-NoOp drops for frontier-era models. All models lose, including the o1 family, which is the most robust.
numbers: GSM-NoOp accuracy change (points): o1-preview -17.5, o1-mini -29.1, GPT-4o -32.0, GPT-4o-mini -40.0, Phi-2 -44.9. Appendix A.5: o1-preview is robust to difficulty changes but still drops on NoOp.
limits: Figure labels were read from extracted text; the exact baseline each is measured against is the GSM-Symbolic base set. Models are 2024.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: by late 2024 the strongest reasoning model still lost 17.5 points to an inert but plausible clause. Whether Claude-5 era models close this is untested here.

source: He et al. (2024) Does Prompt Formatting Have Any Impact on LLM Performance? arXiv 2411.10541
finding: The same content as plain text, Markdown, YAML or JSON gives different accuracy. Best-vs-worst format differences were significant for every model on most benchmarks. Bigger models (GPT-4) are more consistent than GPT-3.5 but not immune, and the best format differs by model.
numbers: GPT-3.5-turbo varies by up to 40% on a code translation task. FIND: GPT-3.5 gains about 200% moving from Markdown to plain text. HumanEval: GPT-4-32k gains over 300% from JSON to plain text. HumanEval-X for one model: YAML 69.8 vs plain 63.0. Consistency between formats (same answer) below 0.5 for GPT-3.5, above 0.5 for GPT-4. Intersection-over-union of best formats across model series often below 0.2.
limits: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 (2023-2024) only, all p-values below 0.05 except GPT-4-1106 on HumanEval. Tasks are MMLU, FIND, HumanEval-X, not layout of rules versus cases.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: any layout test must be run across several equivalent formats and the spread reported. We have no number for our model; the first step is to measure the spread of our own model on 5 to 10 equivalent layouts.

source: Xu et al. (2024) Re-Reading Improves Reasoning in Large Language Models (RE2), arXiv 2309.06275 v4
finding: Repeating the question once ('Read the question again') as input improves reasoning for most models and methods. The authors explain it as a pseudo-bidirectional view in a decoder-only model. Earlier than Leviathan (d06) and consistent with it. Gains are small on strong models and not universal.
numbers: 14 datasets, 112 experiments; arithmetic table: ChatGPT vanilla with RE2 79.45 (+1.66) in the first column. Exceptions noted for a few vanilla ChatGPT scenarios.
limits: Small gains on strong chat models, GPT-3.5 era. Short questions, not long-document tasks.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: second source for the repeat-the-task gain. For a short task, a one-line restatement before reasoning is cheap and low risk.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Thread of Thought Unraveling Chaotic Contexts, arXiv 2311.08734
finding: A plug-in prompt: 'Walk me through this context in manageable parts step by step, summarizing and analyzing as we go', then a second call to extract the answer. It makes the model go through a cluttered context segment by segment. It beat plain, retrieval-only and chain-of-thought prompts on QA with chaotic (many distractors) contexts. It is the nearest relative of a 'link each item to its rule before answering' step, but it does not test rule-to-case linking.
numbers: PopQA exact match with ThoT: GPT-4 0.651, GPT-3.5-turbo 0.674, Llama-2-70B 0.663. EntityQ: 0.643, 0.667, 0.702. Multi-turn persona dialogue score (GPT-3.5 / Llama-2-70B): vanilla 0.398 / 0.330, retrieval 0.475 / 0.510, CoT 0.482 / 0.525, ThoT 0.574 / 0.561. (The rows for the other methods in the PopQA table are scrambled in the extracted text, so only ThoT figures are stated.)
limits: 2023 models, one author group, prompts picked from about 30 candidates. No comparison with a code-side filter. Adds two model calls.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: indirect support only. A walk-through step before answering helps with cluttered input, but nobody has tested an explicit 'match each case to its rule' instruction against placing the rule inline. This stays open.

source: Weston and Sukhbaatar (2023) System 2 Attention, arXiv 2311.11829: limitations section and ablations
finding: Re-read for gap 4. The paper does not measure how often the rewrite drops a needed fact. Its limitations section says S2A 'certainly does not always succeed', costs extra compute because the context is regenerated, and that copying long context is error prone for weaker models, 'although we did not measure this effect clearly'. Ablations: S2A without the instruction, S2A with a single prompt, and S2A that also keeps the original context performed close to full S2A. The instruction-only baseline on GSM-IC did not bring much improvement.
numbers: Factual QA with opinions: instructed prompting 71.7, S2A variants 74.5 to 80.3, baseline 62.8 (see earlier lines b18, c03). Dropped-fact rate: not reported.
quote: it certainly does not always succeed
limits: LLaMA-2-70B-chat, zero-shot prompt not tuned. No code-side filter was compared.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays open: no study found that measures the missed-fact rate of a model rewrite or compares it with a code filter at equal tokens. An audit of our own cleaner (does the needed fact survive?) is a required part of any test.

source: Negative search record for gaps 1, 5, 6 (inline rule vs header; link-before-answer; ID tags) and quota note
finding: No study was found that tests the three cleanest analogues for models: (1) a rule placed inline next to the case versus a separate rules header at equal tokens, (2) an instruction to link each item to its rule before answering versus physical integration, (3) ID tags or colour-style cross-references when referents stay apart. Search was limited: the WebSearch session budget ran out, and arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex answered rate-limit errors (429 and quota) during this session, so this is a weak negative.
numbers: None. Nearest analogues found: premise order (c07), Thread of Thought (d17), NoLiMa answer-option cue (d08), prompt and option repetition (d06, d07).
limits: Absence of evidence after a partly blocked search, not proof that no such study exists. Re-run the search when quotas reset.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1, 5 and 6 stay open and are the best candidates for our own controlled test with the scaffold.

source: Ginns (2006) Integrating information: a meta-analysis of the spatial contiguity and temporal contiguity effects, Learning and Instruction 16 (abstract via ERIC EJ747512; effect sizes via Beege et al. 2019)
finding: The abstract says 50 independent studies, pooling spatial AND temporal contiguity. That explains the size clash in K02: the 0.85 figure belongs to the 50-study pooled set. The 0.72 on 37 effects is most likely the spatial-only subset (our inference, not read). Complexity of the material was a supported moderator.
numbers: Abstract: 50 independent studies, novices. Beege et al. 2019 (full text opened) quote Ginns as weighted mean d = 0.85, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.02, and as d = 0.78 for high-complexity vs d = 0.28 (p > 0.05) for low-complexity material.
quote: for complex learning materials in particular, increasing either the spatial or temporal contiguity of related elements of information can lead to substantial learning gains
limits: Ginns full text could not be opened (publisher 403). The 0.78 vs 0.28 split and the CI are second-hand through Beege. The 37-effect spatial figure is not confirmed.
agent_relevance: Cite 0.85 only as 'spatial plus temporal, 50 studies'. The complexity moderator is the useful part: restructuring should pay off mainly on high element-interactivity items, which supports gating it by the S0 difficulty check.

source: Schroeder and Cenkci (2018) Spatial contiguity and spatial split-attention effects in multimedia learning environments: a meta-analysis, Educational Psychology Review 30 (abstract from publisher landing page and ERIC EJ1186641)
finding: First-hand abstract now read (K01 had it through a German summary). Random-effects pooling of 58 comparisons gives a medium effect for integrated designs, and the abstract says integrated designs helped across many moderators. The abstract mentions no bias correction.
numbers: 58 independent comparisons, n = 2426, g = 0.63, p < 0.001, random effects.
quote: A random effects meta-analysis of 58 independent comparisons (n = 2426) produced an overall effect size of g = 0.63
limits: Full text is paywalled, so publication-bias checks (funnel, trim-and-fill) and the moderator table could not be read. Absence from the abstract is not absence from the paper. Comparisons are mostly text-plus-diagram learning, not text-only prompts.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 stays partly open: the pooled human size is g 0.63, but no bias-corrected size was found in any source we could open.

source: Schroeder (2020) Do measures of cognitive load explain the spatial split-attention principle in multimedia learning environments? A systematic review, Journal of Educational Psychology (abstract via ERIC EJ1240932)
finding: A systematic review of 41 comparisons found that load measures largely do NOT back the extraneous-load explanation. Integrated designs did not clearly change any load measure. The author proposes a different mechanism: integration helps germane, integrative processing.
numbers: 41 comparisons of cognitive-load measures. No compelling evidence that integrated designs lowered any load measure.
limits: Abstract only. Load measures (ratings, secondary tasks) are themselves noisy, so a null may reflect weak measurement.
agent_relevance: The effect may be real but the 'lower extraneous load' story is weak. For the agent: do not assume 'less clutter' works by freeing capacity. Test the integrated layout on accuracy, not on a load story. Supports K07.

source: Beege, Wirzberger, Nebel, Schneider, Schmidt and Rey (2019) Spatial continuity effect vs. spatial contiguity failure, Frontiers in Education 4:86
finding: Full text opened. Experiment 1 had a separated control and three integrated levels (high, medium, low proximity). The planned contrast 'integrated beats separated' failed for retention and transfer. Medium proximity gave the best transfer. The review section notes that studies rarely report how close the 'integrated' condition really was, which may explain mixed results.
numbers: Exp 1 N = 98: contrast integrated vs separated, retention t = 0.66, p = .51; transfer t = 1.47, p = .15; overall condition effect Wilks 0.82, F(6,182) = 3.24, p = .005, partial eta2 = .10. Efficiency contrast p = .74. Quadratic contrast (medium best) t = 3.23, p = .002. Exp 2 N = 85: medium best for retention.
limits: University students, one topic, one lab. The authors list four limitations of Exp 1 (material structure, segment marking). Exploratory.
agent_relevance: Distance is not a simple switch. Closer is not always better, because putting related items close also puts unrelated items close. For prompts: integrate the facts that belong together, but do not interleave unrelated items.

source: Florax and Ploetzner (2010) What contributes to the split-attention effect? Text segmentation, picture labelling and spatial proximity, Learning and Instruction 20 (abstract via ERIC EJ872944)
finding: A 5-group experiment. The split-attention effect showed up for retention only. It was attributed mostly to splitting the text into segments and partly to labelling the picture. Spatial integration itself did not improve learning. This is a named non-replication of the spatial story.
numbers: N = 165 students in five groups (2 x 2 separated with text segmentation x picture labelling, plus one integrated group). Replicated for retention only; comprehension not improved; spatial integration alone n.s.
limits: Abstract only. Single study.
agent_relevance: Part of the integrated-format benefit may come from re-chunking and labelling, not from nearness. For the agent, test 'labelled and chunked' versus 'merely adjacent' as separate arms.

source: Zhang and colleagues (2022, 2023, 2024) split-attention studies with finger pointing and presentation size (ERIC EJ1342341, EJ1387934, EJ1436677)
finding: Recent same-lab results are mixed. 2023: the split-attention effect was confirmed on comprehension and instructional efficiency. 2022: no differences between conditions, including the integrated group. 2024: no effect of format, size or their interaction.
numbers: 2023: N = 129, effect confirmed on comprehension test and efficiency (not on retention). 2022: N = 122, four conditions, no differences on retention, comprehension or load ratings. 2024: N = 146, 2 x 2 format x presentation size, no effects on retention, comprehension or extraneous load.
quote: The present results call for a more nuanced understanding of the split-attention effect
limits: Abstracts only. Same research group. Two of three recent tests are null.
agent_relevance: With Cammeraat 2020 (d01, d02) and Beege 2019 this makes recent human evidence at best mixed. Treat the human analogy as a prompt for testing, not as a proven rule.

source: Test-item settings: Jarodzka et al. (2015) split vs integrated computer-based testing; Moon (2022) spatial integration in geometry items (ERIC EJ1063904, EJ1338781)
finding: A question with a figure is the closest human analogue to a prompt with a task and a source. Jarodzka 2015: students ignored information in the integrated format and worked MORE efficiently in the split format, because the ignored text was mostly irrelevant. Moon 2022: integrating text as diagram labels cut time on task, most for higher prior knowledge.
numbers: Jarodzka: 22 students, half the questions split-screen and half integrated; the integrated format was less efficient. Moon: adults, within-subject integration; efficiency up (time on task down), larger with more prior knowledge.
limits: Abstracts only. Efficiency is time-based in Moon, not accuracy.
agent_relevance: Layout benefit depends on whether the extra text is needed. If the surrounding text is mostly irrelevant, merging it in can cost. Drop the irrelevant text first, then integrate what is left.

source: Lindenbauer, Slinko, Felder, Bogomolov and Zharov (2025) The Complexity Trap: observation masking is as efficient as LLM summarization for agent context management, arXiv 2508.21433 v3
finding: Full text opened. In a tool-using coding agent, hiding old tool outputs behind a placeholder (keep last 10 turns) matches an LLM summary of the history at about half the cost of the raw agent. A strong thinking model got worse with either method. Summaries made runs longer.
numbers: SWE-bench Verified, SWE-agent, turn limit 250, 95% bootstrap CIs. Solve rate raw / masking / summary: Qwen3-32B 17.0 / 15.0 / 16.0; Qwen3-32B thinking 23.0 / 24.6 / 24.8; Qwen3-Coder 480B 53.4 / 54.8 / 53.8; Gemini 2.5 Flash 32.8 / 35.6 / 36.0; Gemini 2.5 Flash thinking 40.4 / 36.4 / 31.4. Masking cost cut 41 to 57% in 4 of 5 setups (Qwen3-32B thinking only 9.8%). Mean turns for Gemini Flash: raw 50, masking 44, summary 52 (+15% vs masking). Hybrid (summary after N=43 turns, window 10) on Verified-50, Qwen3-Coder: cost 7% below masking and 11% below summary, +2.6 points vs raw.
limits: Only software-engineering tool outputs, which are long and verbose. Window M=10 is tuned per scaffold. Hybrid tested on a 50-instance subset only. Confidence intervals overlap in most rows, so 'equal' means 'not shown different'.
agent_relevance: For gap 9: masking old observations is a cheap default for the agent loop. Summaries cost a call and can lengthen runs. Thinking models may need the full history. This is dollars, not an equal-token test, and fresh-context attempts (S3) were not studied.

source: Yang, Huang, Zhang, Surdeanu, Wang and Pan (2025) How is LLM reasoning distracted by irrelevant context? GSM-DC, arXiv 2505.18761 v2
finding: A synthetic math benchmark where irrelevant nodes are injected into a symbolic graph without changing the answer. Accuracy of the reasoning steps falls steadily as irrelevant context grows, for 2025 models. Training on hard distractors helps.
numbers: Six instruct models (Grok-3-Beta, GPT-4.1, GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.3-70B, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.2-1B), 100 instances per condition, 5-shot. At reasoning depth 5: Grok-3-Beta step accuracy 43% with 1 irrelevant item to 19% with 15; GPT-4.1 26% to 2%.
limits: Synthetic symbolic problems, no reasoning-mode models in the main table. Step accuracy is a strict all-or-nothing metric.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 4: even 2025 non-reasoning frontier models lose a lot on deep problems when irrelevant items are added. Cutting irrelevant items in code before the call is a cheap lever.

source: Gema et al. (2025) Inverse scaling in test-time compute, TMLR (arXiv 2507.14417 v2)
finding: Longer reasoning can make reasoning models worse on tasks with irrelevant distractors. Claude models get more distracted as they reason longer. OpenAI o-series resists distractors but overfits to framing. DeepSeek R1 collapses in the natural-length setting.
numbers: Counting tasks with 1 to 5 inserted distractors (500 questions per count). Claude Opus 4: near 100% accuracy falls to about 85 to 90% as reasoning extends. DeepSeek R1 natural overthinking: 70% to 30% at five distractors. o3 stable in the controlled setup, weak trend in the natural setup. 95% CIs shown.
limits: Simple counting questions built to be easy, so the size reflects a stress test, not typical work. Results shown mostly in figures.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 answered in part: strong reasoning models still lose accuracy to inert clauses, and extra thinking does not rescue them. Argues for removing distractors before reasoning rather than asking the model to ignore them.

source: Shi et al. (2023) Large language models can be easily distracted by irrelevant context (GSM-IC), arXiv 2302.00093: breakdown by distractor type
finding: Re-opened for gap 8. Distractor sentences that are on the same topic, reuse the role name from the problem, and use numbers in the range of the real ones hurt most. Problems needing four or more steps lose more under chain-of-thought, while least-to-most prompting stays flat across step count.
numbers: Self-consistency with 20 samples raised micro accuracy by more than 11 points (35.5 points on 0-COT); best macro accuracy among all prompting methods only 45%; correct answer in the 20 samples for 99.7% of problems.
limits: Older models (code-davinci-002, text-davinci-003). Figures hold the step-count curves; the text gives the pattern only. Arithmetic word problems only.
agent_relevance: Near-miss text is the dangerous kind in reasoning, as in retrieval (d31). Code can drop distractors that share names and number ranges with the task, but that is a heuristic, not tested here. Step count works as a proxy for element interactivity (gap 7).

source: Cuconasu et al. (2024) The Power of Noise: Redefining retrieval for RAG systems, SIGIR 2024 (arXiv 2401.14887 v4)
finding: Re-opened for gap 8. Related-but-wrong documents hurt a lot. Random, unrelated documents added alongside the relevant ones raised accuracy. The authors suggest the noise conditions the attention.
numbers: Distracting (related, no answer) documents: accuracy deteriorates by more than 0.38 (-67%) as their number grows; one distractor alone gives a drop of up to 0.24 (-25%). Random documents on NQ-open with Llama2-7b: gain up to 0.07 (+35%) with 4 retrieved documents.
limits: Old open models (Llama2, Falcon, Phi-2, MPT), retrieval QA, one specific placement of random documents. Not a reasoning task.
agent_relevance: Near-miss beats random in harm. Random filler may be harmless or even helpful, so the rule is 'remove near-misses', not 'remove all extra text'. Gap 8 answered for retrieval QA, partly for reasoning (d28, d30).

source: Chen, Chi, Wang and Zhou (2024) Premise order matters in reasoning with large language models, arXiv 2402.08939 v3
finding: Putting the facts in the order they are used in the proof beats a shuffled order. Reordering a relevant set of rules can cost over 30 points on logic tasks. This is the closest direct test of 'related things should be adjacent' in text, though it tests order, not integration.
numbers: Logic: forward vs shuffled order drops of 20 to 30 points for GPT-4-turbo and PaLM 2-L, over 40 points (from over 65% to below 25%) for Gemini 1.0 Pro and GPT-3.5-turbo. R-GSM (220 pairs): GPT-4-turbo 94.1 to 85.0 on all; 100 to 89.9 on the subset solved originally; GPT-3.5-turbo 67.3 to 51.8.
limits: 2024-era models, no reasoning-mode models. Order is the manipulation, not inline versus header.
agent_relevance: Layout tests must control for order. If we test integrated vs separated, keep the use-order the same in both arms, or an order effect will be mistaken for an integration effect.

source: Li et al. (2024) GSM-Plus: a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating the robustness of LLMs as mathematical problem solvers, arXiv 2402.19255
finding: Eight kinds of question variations on GSM8K, including distractor insertion (topic-related extra statements) and critical thinking (an essential statement removed). Humans lose nothing. Models lose accuracy, and larger models resist distractors better.
numbers: Performance drop rate overall: human -2.05%, GPT-4 8.23%, GPT-3.5-Turbo 16.88%, LLaMA-2-13B 34.76%. GPT-4 85.58 on GSM-Plus vs 93.25 on GSM8K. Distractor insertion drop rates named in text: MAmmoTH-13B 40.6%, SEGO-13B 43.9%, MetaMath-13B 39.4%, Abel-13B 31.8%; GPT-4 distractor-only rate is in a figure.
limits: Old models, and the distractor-only drop for GPT-4 is not stated in text.
agent_relevance: Confirms the Shi pattern with a human baseline: people are not hurt but models are. 'Models are like humans here' is false for inert text.

source: Jaroslawicz et al. (2025) How many instructions can LLMs follow at once? IFScale, arXiv 2507.11538
finding: Instruction-following falls as the number of instructions in one prompt rises. Reasoning models hold near-perfect until a threshold, other models decay linearly or exponentially. Earlier instructions are followed better, but the bias fades at extreme density.
numbers: 20 models, up to 500 keyword-inclusion instructions, 5 runs. Best frontier accuracy at 500 instructions about 68%; o3 62.8%, grok-3 61.9%, claude-3.7-sonnet 52.7%, claude-opus-4 44.6%, claude-sonnet-4 42.9%, deepseek-r1 30.9%, qwen3 26.9%. Primacy ratio peaks around 150 to 200 instructions.
limits: One synthetic task (business report with keywords). Not a split-attention test. Many instructions are not the same as extra irrelevant text.
agent_relevance: Rule density is a budget. Our guardrails G1 to G12 and operators should stay few and short. Put the most important rules first.

source: Hsieh et al. (2024) RULER: what's the real context size of your long-context language models? COLM 2024 (arXiv 2404.06654 v3)
finding: Even when the haystack is built for the task (multi-hop, aggregation), accuracy falls with length. Claimed context sizes overstate usable size. For gap 4: length alone costs strong 2024 models only a few points at agent lengths, much more beyond 64K.
limits: Synthetic tasks where most of the haystack is filler, so 'clean relevant context' is not isolated. 2024 models. No 2025-2026 models.
agent_relevance: At agent lengths (5K to 30K) strong models lose a few points from length itself. Do not over-trim useful context for fear of length. The larger losses come from near-miss content and reasoning depth.

source: Voronov, Wolf and Ryabinin (2024) Mind your format, arXiv 2401.06766; with Chatterjee et al. (2024) POSIX prompt sensitivity index, arXiv 2410.02185
finding: Gap 10: prompt template alone moves accuracy a lot. A poor template can drop strong models to random guessing, and the best template does not carry over between models, even in one family. Template differences can swamp method differences.
numbers: 21 models (770M to 70B), 4 classification datasets: poor template reduces the strongest models to random-guess level; even the largest models show standard deviations up to 35% of their mean across templates. Example-selection methods often lose to random choice once template spread is counted. POSIX: template changes give the highest sensitivity on multiple-choice tasks; one few-shot exemplar almost always lowers sensitivity.
limits: Classification tasks and older open models. Sensitivity of current frontier chat models on our own prompt format is not measured.
agent_relevance: Run every layout comparison over several templates and seeds. Ignore any gap smaller than the template spread we measure ourselves. Adding one worked example may cut sensitivity.

source: Search record for this gap pass (2026-10-31): direct LLM tests of integrated vs separated sources; Chandler and Sweller 1992 full text; bias-corrected human effect
finding: No LLM study of the classic integrated-vs-separated contrast was found. Chandler and Sweller 1992 could not be opened (publisher 403; ERIC and e-teaching.org give only bibliographic data). No bias-corrected human effect was found. Web search quota was spent and arXiv and OpenAlex API calls were rate-limited, so the negative is weaker than a full search.
numbers: None.
limits: This is a failed search, not proof of absence. ERIC API, Crossref, Springer landing pages and direct arXiv PDFs worked; Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex and arXiv export did not.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 stays open and is the first thing to test on our own harness: same facts, same tokens, inline vs header, several templates, several seeds.
